notes.b: Economic activity such as farming, fishing, mining and industry always affects the environment. Sustainable development is the framework within which that environmental impact is controlled.
points: The Brundtland Report, "Our Common Future" (UN World Commission on Environment and Development, 1987), defined it as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

It has three pillars: environmental protection, economic growth and social fairness. Sustainable development balances all three rather than maximising one, so a plan that boosts profit but wrecks the environment is not sustainable.
notes.tip: The Brundtland Report (1987) gave the definition. The Rio Earth Summit (1992) was a separate, later event, so do not mix them up. Short questions ask what is meant by sustainable development, so learn the definition and the three pillars.

notes.b: Five working rules turn the definition into practice. Each one protects the environment so that it can keep supporting people in the future.
points: Renewable resources (ones that regrow or refill naturally) such as fish, forests and water should be used no faster than they regenerate, otherwise they are used up.
Non-renewable resources (ones that cannot be replaced once used) should be used efficiently and recycled, so that they last longer.
Pollution should be kept within what the environment can absorb, so that air, water and soil are not overloaded.
The polluter pays: those who cause environmental damage bear the cost of it, which gives them a reason to cause less.
The precautionary principle: act to prevent serious harm even before the harm is proven, because waiting for proof may be too late.

notes.b: Sustainable development became an international aim, with world meetings setting out plans for governments to follow.
points: The Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (1992) was a later, separate event from the Brundtland Report. It produced Agenda 21, an action plan for sustainable development.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2015: 17 goals with a target year of 2030.
notes.tip: Do not say the Rio Earth Summit defined sustainable development. That was the Brundtland Report in 1987, and Rio came later in 1992.

notes.b: In Ireland, the main body that controls the environmental impact of industry is the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). It was created by law and works independently of the government departments it advises.
points: It was set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992, and the EPA began work in 1993.
It is an independent public body (a State organisation not run by a government minister) with headquarters at Johnstown Castle, Co. Wexford.
notes.tip: Short questions ask about the role of the EPA. Remember that the EPA licenses emissions but does not grant planning permission.

notes.b: The EPA's most important power is licensing. Activities with a high risk of pollution may not operate unless the EPA allows it and sets the conditions.
points: Large industries need an EPA licence: pharmaceutical and chemical plants, power stations, intensive pig and poultry farms, cement works and mines. Waste facilities also need one.
The licence sets emission limits for the activity, which means the maximum pollution it may release into air, water or land.
Integrated pollution control means one licence covers air, water, waste and noise, instead of separate permits for each. This lets the EPA look at the whole impact of a site at once.
notes.tip: The EPA licenses emissions. It does not grant planning permission: local authorities and An Coimisiún Pleanála do that.

notes.b: To control pollution, the EPA first has to measure it. It tracks the state of the environment and reports what it finds.
points: The EPA monitors water quality in rivers, lakes, estuaries (where rivers meet the sea), groundwater (water held underground in rock and soil) and bathing waters.
It runs a national air quality network and produces a greenhouse gas inventory (a count of emissions of gases that cause climate change) and projections of future emissions.
Drinking water is supplied by Uisce Éireann.
The State of the Environment report is published every four years, so the public and government can see whether things are improving.
The EPA advises government and the public and funds environmental research.
The EPA took over radiological protection in 2014, including the control of radon (a natural radioactive gas that can seep up from the ground).

notes.b: A licence is only useful if it is obeyed, so the EPA checks and punishes breaches.
points: Inspections check that licensed activities keep within their emission limits.
The Office of Environmental Enforcement, set up within the EPA in 2003, prosecutes polluters (takes them to court).
The EPA oversees the environmental work carried out by local authorities (the county and city councils).

notes.b: The EPA cannot solve every problem alone. Some pollution is hard to see, track or assign to one source.
points: The EPA cannot inspect everywhere, so some breaches go unchecked.
Diffuse pollution (pollution that comes from many scattered sources rather than one pipe or chimney) from thousands of farms is hard to police.
Local authorities and other bodies share responsibility for environmental control, so the EPA is one part of a wider system.

notes.h: Environmental impact assessment: what it is
notes.b: Control is best done before a project starts. An environmental impact assessment is the study that looks at a project's likely effects in advance.
points: An environmental impact assessment is a study, required before planning permission is decided for large projects, that predicts a project's effects on the environment and how to reduce them.
The developer's report (the developer is the company or body proposing the project) was called an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). It is now an Environmental Impact Assessment Report (EIAR).
notes.tip: The developer writes the EIS or EIAR, often with consultants. It is not written by the EPA or the planning authority.

notes.b: Environmental impact assessment is not optional for big projects. It comes from EU law and is built into Irish planning rules.
points: The EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, 1985, is applied in Irish planning law.

Assessment is required for projects above set sizes, such as motorways, power stations, wind farms, mines and quarries, large intensive farms, pipelines, ports and airports. Small projects below the set sizes do not need one.

notes.b: An EIAR has to describe the project, the place it will be built and every kind of effect it could have, then say how harm will be reduced.
points: A description of the project and of the existing environment (the baseline, meaning the condition of the site before anything is built, which later effects are measured against).
Likely effects on people, plants and animals, soil, water, air, climate, landscape, archaeology and heritage, traffic and noise.
Alternatives considered, such as other designs or sites, and the mitigation measures (steps to reduce or prevent harm) proposed to reduce effects.
A non-technical summary for the public, so ordinary people can understand the report.
The developer writes the report, often with consultants. Neither the EPA nor the planning authority writes it.

notes.b: The assessment follows a set order. It ends with a decision-maker who weighs the report against what the public and experts say.
points: 1. The developer prepares the EIAR.
2. The public and bodies such as the National Parks and Wildlife Service make submissions (written comments and objections).

3. The planning authority or An Coimisiún Pleanála decides whether to grant permission, often with conditions. The board was renamed in 2025 from An Bord Pleanála, the national planning appeals board.
notes.tip: Be clear who does what. The developer prepares the report, and the planning authority or An Coimisiún Pleanála decides. The EPA does neither.

notes.h: Why environmental impact studies are necessary
notes.b: Short questions ask why environmental impact studies are needed. There are four reasons, and Ireland's experience at Derrybrien shows what happens when the law is not followed.
points: They prevent damage before it happens, which is cheaper than paying for clean-up afterwards.
They require developers to consider alternatives, so a less harmful design or site may be chosen.
They give the public a say in decisions, through submissions.
They are a legal requirement.

At Derrybrien, Co. Galway, a peat slide on 16 October 2003 occurred during wind-farm construction. In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out.
notes.tip: Use Derrybrien as the example of the legal requirement: Ireland was fined because no proper assessment was done.

notes.b: Fish are a renewable resource, but only if people leave enough of them to breed. This idea is the basis of sustainable fishing.
points: Fish are renewable only while catches stay below the rate at which the stock (the population of one kind of fish) breeds and grows.
The maximum sustainable yield is the largest catch that can be taken year after year without reducing the stock.

notes.b: Overfishing means taking fish faster than stocks can replace themselves. Several causes push fleets to do this.
points: Modern technology, including sonar (finds fish using sound), satellite navigation, factory ships (which process the catch at sea) and huge nets, lets fleets find and take fish faster than stocks can recover.
Too many boats chase the same stock, so the catch is shared out among more boats and each one fishes harder.
Subsidies (payments from government) keep fleets fishing when stocks are falling.
Young fish are caught before they have had the chance to breed, so the stock cannot renew itself.
Discards: dead or unwanted fish are thrown back into the sea, which wastes the catch.
Illegal fishing takes fish outside the quota system (the limits on how much each country or boat may catch).

notes.h: Past experience: Grand Banks cod collapse, Newfoundland
notes.b: The Grand Banks is the classic example of a fishery destroyed by overfishing. It shows how both fish stocks and jobs can be lost.
points: The Grand Banks, off Newfoundland, Canada, were one of the world's richest cod fisheries for centuries.
Catches rose sharply with factory trawlers (large boats that fish with nets and process the catch on board) from the 1960s, and the stock collapsed.
Canada declared a moratorium (ban) on northern cod fishing on 2 July 1992.
About 30,000 people in Newfoundland lost their jobs, the largest single lay-off in Canadian history.
The stock has recovered only slowly, and partly, in the decades since.
notes.tip: The Grand Banks are off Canada, not in EU waters. Remember the moratorium date, 2 July 1992, and say about 30,000 jobs.

notes.b: North Sea herring is a second example, with a happier ending. It shows that a stock can recover when fishing is stopped and then tightly limited.
points: North Sea herring was overfished in the 1960s and 1970s.
The fishery was closed from 1977 to the early 1980s, which gave the stock time to breed.
The stock recovered after the fishery reopened under strict quotas.

notes.h: Managing fish stocks: the Common Fisheries Policy
notes.b: In EU waters, fish stocks are managed through the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP). Here it matters as a conservation tool that tries to keep catches sustainable.
points: The EU Common Fisheries Policy, 1983, sets total allowable catches (TACs, the maximum amount of each stock that may be caught) and divides them into national quotas.
Conservation rules include minimum mesh sizes (so small fish escape the net), minimum landing sizes, closed areas and seasons, and vessel decommissioning (scrapping boats to reduce fleet size).
The CFP reform of 2013 aims to fish at maximum sustainable yield and introduces a landing obligation that ends discards, phased in from 2015 to 2019.
Monitoring uses satellite tracking, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (set up in 2007) and fishery protection patrols by the Irish Naval Service.
Ireland's exclusive economic zone (the sea area over which a country controls resources) extends 200 nautical miles from the coast, within which these rules apply.
Further measures include marine protected areas (areas of sea where fishing is restricted) and aquaculture (fish farming) as an alternative to wild catch.
notes.tip: Here the CFP is a sustainability case, so write about its conservation measures. Do not write about its effect on the Irish economy.

notes.b: Fishing matters to Irish coastal communities, which depend on the fish stocks around the coast for their living.
points: Mackerel is the most valuable Irish catch, landed mainly at Killybegs, Co. Donegal, Ireland's largest fishing port.
Killybegs is the base of the pelagic fleet (boats that fish species living in open water, not on the seabed) that catches mackerel and herring.
Ireland has six State Fishery Harbour Centres: Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel, Dunmore East and Howth.
Irish fishing communities depend on these stocks, so conservation limits cause hardship. There is more on this in Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests.

notes.h: Mining sites: Avoca, past experience without controls
notes.b: Mining that happened before modern controls can go on polluting for generations. Avoca is the Irish example.
points: Copper mining at Avoca, Co. Wicklow, over centuries left acid mine drainage (acidic water that runs out of old mine workings) when mining ended.
The acid drainage still discolours and pollutes the Avoca River long after the mines closed, which shows why closure plans are needed.
notes.tip: Here the focus is on control, licensing and rehabilitation of mines. Use Avoca as the case with no controls, with pollution lasting long after closure.

notes.h: Mining sites: Tara Mines, present practice
notes.b: Today a mine has to work within licence rules. Tara Mines shows what controlled mining looks like.
points: Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is an underground zinc and lead mine, Europe's largest zinc mine, producing since 1977 and owned by Boliden.
It operates under an EPA licence, which sets limits on its emissions.
Tailings (the waste left after the metal has been extracted) are stored in a lined tailings facility, so they do not leak into the ground, and the water is monitored.
Restoration plans are in place for the site.

notes.h: Mining sites: Lisheen, rehabilitation after closure
notes.b: A responsible mine plans for its end before it opens. Lisheen shows rehabilitation (restoring a site to a safe, useful condition) after closure.
points: Lisheen, Co. Tipperary, a zinc and lead mine, closed in 2015 and the site has been rehabilitated.

A new mine needs an environmental impact assessment report (EIAR) and a closure and restoration plan backed by a financial bond (money set aside in advance) before it opens, so the clean-up is paid for even if the company fails.

notes.b: Peat was long treated as a fuel to be dug out. The scale of that harvesting damaged Ireland's bogs.
points: Bord na Móna, founded in 1946, carried out large-scale industrial harvesting of peat for power stations and fuel.
Harvesting removed raised bogs (domed peatlands formed over thousands of years), released the carbon they had stored and destroyed their habitats.

notes.b: Peat harvesting has ended, and the focus has moved to repairing the damage and finding new uses for the land.
points: The Lanesborough and Shannonbridge peat stations closed in December 2020, and Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting in January 2021.
Cutaway bogs (bogs where the peat has been removed) are being rehabilitated and rewetted, meaning water is returned to them.
Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly: a cutaway bog turned into parkland, wetlands and trails.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo: the peat station closed in 2003 and wind farms now stand on the cutaway bog.
A just transition (a change that is fair to the workers affected) is needed for Midland workers who lost jobs in peat.

notes.h: Global past experience: the Aral Sea
notes.b: The Aral Sea shows how diverting water for farming can destroy a whole environment and the livelihoods that depended on it.
points: The Amu Darya and Syr Darya, which feed the Aral Sea in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, were diverted from the 1960s to irrigate (water by channels) cotton in the Soviet Union.
The sea shrank to a fraction of its size and split into separate lakes, and its salinity (salt content) rose.
The fishing industry collapsed, and ports such as Moynaq (Uzbekistan) were left stranded far from the water.
Dust storms spread salt and pesticides from the exposed seabed, harming local health.
The Kok-Aral dam (Kazakhstan, 2005) raised the level of the small northern sea, and fishing there has partly revived.

notes.b: Burning fossil fuels pollutes the air and adds to climate change, so a sustainable approach changes the energy source.
points: Switching to renewable energy (energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind) reduces the environmental impact of power generation. There is more on this in Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources.

notes.b: Farming can be paid and encouraged to protect the environment, not just to produce food.
points: Agri-environment schemes pay farmers for conservation: REPS (Rural Environment Protection Scheme, 1994), now succeeded by ACRES.
Origin Green, Bord Bia's sustainability programme for Irish food and drink, was launched in 2012.
Nitrates rules limit the amount of nitrogen fertiliser and manure that farms can apply, because the excess can run off and pollute water.
BurrenLIFE (2005 to 2010) paid Burren farmers to manage species-rich limestone grassland through winter grazing (winterage); it continued as the Burren Programme.
Results-based farming in the Burren rewards farmers for measured environmental outcomes, not just for following set practices.

notes.b: Forests and tourist sites can be used without being destroyed if how they are used is controlled.
points: Forests are replanted after felling, using mixed native broadleaves (a variety of native trees such as oak, rather than one species).
Forests are not planted on deep peat.
Visitor limits and ecotourism (tourism designed to protect nature) reduce pressure on fragile sites.
At Skellig Michael, Co. Kerry, access is controlled through licensed boats and visitor limits.

notes.b: The best way to deal with waste is to create less of it, which is why there is an order of priority.
points: Reduce, reuse and recycle, in that order of priority.
Levies (charges) and deposit schemes (a refundable payment on containers) give people and businesses an incentive to reduce waste.
A circular economy keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible, instead of using them once and throwing them away.

notes.b: The polluter pays principle is put into effect through taxes and charges that put a price on pollution.
points: Irish carbon tax, introduced in 2010.
Plastic bag levy, introduced in March 2002, a charge on plastic bags, so shoppers have a reason to use fewer.
Landfill levy, charged on waste sent to landfill, so dumping costs more than reducing waste.
EU Emissions Trading System, from 2005: companies pay for the emissions they release.

notes.b: Governments have set targets for cutting emissions, and the future of sustainable development depends on meeting them.
points: The EU and Ireland aim for climate neutrality by 2050 (releasing no more greenhouse gases than are removed).
Ireland's Climate Act 2021 sets a 51% cut in emissions by 2030.
The Climate Action Plan sets 80% renewable electricity by 2030 and a retrofit (upgrading insulation and heating) of 500,000 homes to B2 energy rating by 2030.
Offshore wind, electric vehicles, public transport and the circular economy are the main routes to lower emissions.
Cutting agricultural emissions, restoring bogs and planting forests as carbon sinks (places that absorb and store carbon).
notes.tip: Higher Level 30-mark questions ask how economic activities can be developed sustainably to control their environmental impact. Finish with future prospects after the definition, the EPA, environmental impact assessment and named activities.

notes.b: Meeting these targets will not be easy. Several obstacles stand in the way.
points: Cost: clean technology, retrofitting and rehabilitation are expensive.
Short-term economic pressure favours quick profit over long-term protection.
Jobs in traditional industries, such as peat and fishing, are at risk.
Global cooperation is needed, because pollution and climate change do not stop at borders.

keyTerms.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The principle of acting to prevent serious environmental harm even before the harm has been proven.
A single EPA licence that sets limits for emissions to air, water, waste and noise together.
A study of a large project's likely effects on the environment and of the measures to reduce them, required before planning permission is decided.
The largest catch that can be taken from a fish stock year after year without reducing the stock.
The maximum quantity of a fish stock that may be caught in a year, divided into national quotas under the Common Fisheries Policy.
Fish caught and thrown back dead or unwanted, which the landing obligation of the 2013 CFP reform aims to end.
The waste rock and fine material left over after minerals are extracted from ore, stored in a managed facility at a mine.
An economic model that keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling.

factCards.term: Sustainable development: who defined it, its pillars and global framework
factCards.definition: Defined in the Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987); it balances environmental protection, economic growth and social fairness. The later Rio Earth Summit (1992) produced Agenda 21; the UN Sustainable Development Goals (2015) set 17 goals for 2030.

factCards.term: The EPA: when and how it was set up
factCards.definition: Set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992 and began work in 1993; an independent public body with its headquarters at Johnstown Castle, Co. Wexford.

factCards.term: EPA licensing: who needs a licence and what it covers
factCards.definition: Large industries (pharmaceutical and chemical plants, power stations, intensive pig and poultry farms, cement works, mines) and waste facilities; the licence sets emission limits, and one licence covers air, water, waste and noise.

factCards.term: EPA monitoring and reporting: four roles
factCards.definition: Monitors rivers, lakes, estuaries, groundwater and bathing waters; runs the national air quality network and greenhouse gas inventory; publishes a State of the Environment report every four years; radiological protection, including radon, since 2014.

factCards.term: EPA enforcement and the limits of its control
factCards.definition: Inspections; the Office of Environmental Enforcement (2003) prosecutes polluters; oversight of local authorities. Limits: it cannot inspect everywhere, diffuse pollution from thousands of farms is hard to police, and local authorities share responsibility.

factCards.term: Environmental impact assessment: legal basis and projects covered
factCards.definition: The EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (1985), applied in Irish planning law, requires one for projects above set sizes: motorways, power stations, wind farms, mines and quarries, large intensive farms, pipelines, ports and airports.

factCards.term: EIAR: what the report must contain
factCards.definition: A description of the project; the existing environment (baseline); likely effects on people, wildlife, soil, water, air, climate, landscape, heritage, traffic and noise; alternatives considered; mitigation measures; a non-technical summary for the public.

factCards.term: Environmental impact assessment: the three-step process
factCards.definition: First the developer, often with consultants, prepares the EIAR; then the public and bodies such as the National Parks and Wildlife Service make submissions; finally the planning authority or An Coimisiún Pleanála (An Bord Pleanála until 2025) decides.

factCards.term: Why environmental impact studies are necessary: four reasons
factCards.definition: They prevent damage before it happens, which is cheaper than clean-up; they make developers consider alternatives; they give the public a say; they are legally required, as the Derrybrien case shows.

factCards.term: Derrybrien, Co. Galway: the cost of no proper EIA
factCards.definition: A peat slide occurred on 16 October 2003 during wind-farm construction on bog. In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out.

factCards.term: Overfishing: six causes
factCards.definition: Modern technology (sonar, satellite navigation, factory ships, huge nets); too many boats chasing the same stock; subsidies that keep fleets fishing; young fish caught before they breed; discards; illegal fishing outside the quota system.

factCards.term: Grand Banks cod collapse, Newfoundland: what happened and the effects
factCards.definition: Catches rose sharply with factory trawlers from the 1960s and the stock collapsed; Canada banned northern cod fishing on 2 July 1992; about 30,000 people lost their jobs, the largest single lay-off in Canadian history; recovery has been slow and partial.

factCards.term: North Sea herring: collapse and recovery
factCards.definition: Overfished in the 1960s and 1970s; the fishery was closed from 1977 to the early 1980s; the stock recovered after the fishery reopened under strict quotas.

factCards.term: Common Fisheries Policy: five conservation measures
factCards.definition: CFP (1983): total allowable catches divided into national quotas; minimum mesh and landing sizes; closed areas and seasons; vessel decommissioning; marine protected areas, with aquaculture as an alternative to wild catch.

factCards.term: CFP 2013 reform and monitoring in Irish waters
factCards.definition: The 2013 reform: fish at maximum sustainable yield and a landing obligation ending discards, phased in 2015 to 2019. Monitoring by satellite, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (2007) and Naval Service patrols within the 200-nautical-mile zone.

factCards.term: Irish fishing: most valuable catch and main port
factCards.definition: Mackerel is the most valuable Irish catch, landed mainly at Killybegs, Co. Donegal, Ireland's largest fishing port and base of the pelagic fleet. Conservation limits cause hardship for fishing communities that depend on the stocks.

factCards.term: Mining past and present: Avoca compared with Tara Mines
factCards.definition: Avoca, Co. Wicklow: centuries of copper mining left acid mine drainage that still pollutes the Avoca River. Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, Europe's largest zinc mine: EPA licence, lined tailings facility, water monitoring, restoration plans.

factCards.term: Mine rehabilitation: Lisheen and the rules for new mines
factCards.definition: Lisheen, Co. Tipperary, a zinc and lead mine, closed in 2015 and its site was rehabilitated. A new mine needs an EIAR and a closure and restoration plan backed by a financial bond before it opens.

factCards.term: Peatlands: from industrial harvesting to restoration
factCards.definition: Bord na Móna (1946) harvesting removed raised bogs, released stored carbon and destroyed habitats. Harvesting ended in January 2021; cutaway bogs are rewetted or reused (Lough Boora parkland, Bellacorick wind farms); Midland workers need a just transition.

factCards.term: Aral Sea: what was done and what happened to the sea
factCards.definition: From the 1960s the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, which feed the Aral Sea (Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan), were diverted to irrigate cotton in the Soviet Union; the sea shrank to a fraction of its size, split into separate lakes and grew saltier.

factCards.term: Aral Sea: effects on people and the partial recovery
factCards.definition: Fishing collapsed; ports such as Moynaq (Uzbekistan) were stranded far from the water; dust storms spread salt and pesticides, harming health. The Kok-Aral dam (Kazakhstan, 2005) raised the small northern sea, and fishing there has partly revived.

factCards.term: Sustainable farming in Ireland: name three schemes
factCards.definition: REPS (Rural Environment Protection Scheme, 1994), now ACRES; Origin Green, Bord Bia's sustainability programme (2012); BurrenLIFE (2005 to 2010), which paid Burren farmers to manage limestone grassland by winter grazing, now the Burren Programme.

factCards.term: The polluter pays: four examples in Ireland
factCards.definition: The Irish carbon tax (2010); the plastic bag levy (March 2002); the landfill levy on waste sent to landfill; the EU Emissions Trading System (2005), under which companies pay for the emissions they release.

factCards.term: Sustainable development: four obstacles
factCards.definition: Cost: clean technology, retrofitting and rehabilitation are expensive; short-term economic pressure favours quick profit; jobs in traditional industries such as peat and fishing are at risk; global cooperation is needed because pollution crosses borders.

questions.prompt: Examine how economic activities can be developed sustainably in order to control their environmental impact.
questions.model: Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising future generations, balancing environmental protection, economic growth and social fairness. The Environmental Protection Agency controls the impact of economic activity by licensing large industries and waste facilities, setting emission limits under integrated pollution control, monitoring water, air and greenhouse gases, and enforcing licences through inspections and prosecution by the Office of Environmental Enforcement. Environmental impact assessment requires the developer to prepare an EIAR before planning permission is decided, describing the existing environment, likely effects, alternatives and mitigation measures, and the public can make submissions. Fish stocks must be fished below maximum sustainable yield. Overfishing on the Grand Banks, Newfoundland, led to a cod moratorium on 2 July 1992 and about 30,000 job losses, while North Sea herring was closed from 1977 and recovered under strict quotas. The Common Fisheries Policy sets total allowable catches, mesh sizes, closed areas and a landing obligation to end discards, and satellite monitoring, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority and Naval Service patrols enforce them. Mining shows the progression from control to rehabilitation: Avoca's acid mine drainage shows the damage of uncontrolled mining, Tara Mines operates under an EPA licence with a lined tailings facility and water monitoring, and Lisheen was rehabilitated after its closure in 2015, while new mines need a closure plan with a financial bond. Other activities are made more sustainable by renewable energy, agri-environment schemes such as REPS and ACRES, Origin Green, and polluter-pays measures such as the carbon tax. Future prospects include climate neutrality by 2050 and a 51% emissions cut by 2030, but cost, short-term pressure and job losses in traditional industries remain obstacles.

questions.prompt: Discuss the role of the Environmental Protection Agency and of environmental impact assessment in controlling the environmental impact of economic activity.
questions.model: The EPA was set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992, began work in 1993 and has its headquarters at Johnstown Castle, Co. Wexford. It controls environmental impact by licensing large industries and waste facilities and setting their emission limits through integrated pollution control. It monitors rivers, lakes, estuaries, groundwater, bathing waters, air quality and greenhouse gases, and it enforces licences through inspections and prosecutions, with the Office of Environmental Enforcement set up in 2003. It publishes the State of the Environment report every four years and advises government. Its limits are that it cannot be everywhere, diffuse pollution from thousands of farms is hard to police, and local authorities share responsibility. Environmental impact assessment, required under the EU directive of 1985, is needed before planning permission is decided for large projects. The developer prepares an EIAR describing the baseline environment, the likely effects, alternatives and mitigation measures, and the public and bodies such as the National Parks and Wildlife Service make submissions before the planning authority or An Coimisiún Pleanála decides. It is necessary because it prevents damage before it happens, gives the public a say and is a legal requirement. Derrybrien, Co. Galway, shows the cost of skipping it: after a peat slide on 16 October 2003 during wind-farm construction, the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland €5 million plus €15,000 a day in 2019.

questions.prompt: Explain how the depletion of fish stocks can be prevented, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Fish stocks are renewable only if catches stay below the maximum sustainable yield, but modern technology such as sonar, satellite navigation and factory ships, too many boats, subsidies, catching young fish before they breed, discards and illegal fishing have depleted stocks. Prevention begins with the Common Fisheries Policy, which sets total allowable catches divided into national quotas, with mesh sizes, minimum landing sizes, closed areas and seasons, and vessel decommissioning. The 2013 reform aims to fish at maximum sustainable yield and introduces a landing obligation to end discards. The Grand Banks cod collapsed after factory trawlers arrived in the 1960s, and the moratorium of 2 July 1992 cost about 30,000 jobs, showing the cost of failing to act. North Sea herring recovered after the fishery was closed from 1977 and reopened under strict quotas. In Irish waters, satellite monitoring, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority and Naval Service patrols enforce the rules across the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, and marine protected areas and aquaculture offer alternatives.
